panels.bubble_text: FORTRAN changed everything. Code that looked like math.
panels.speaker: PIXEL

panels.text: John Warner Backus was a 29-year-old programmer at IBM who hated programming. Not the problem-solving — he hated the tedium. In 1953, he proposed a radical project: build a language where scientists could write formulas that looked like actual mathematics. He called it FORTRAN — short for FORmula TRANslation.

panels.caption: One FORTRAN line replaces many assembly instructions

panels.text: The skeptics were fierce. Assembly programmers argued no compiler could produce code as efficient as a skilled human. Backus and his team spent enormous effort on an optimizing compiler — one that translated cleverly. According to IBM's benchmarks, FORTRAN programs ran roughly as fast as hand-written assembly. Within two years, over half of all new IBM 704 code was written in FORTRAN.

panels.text: FORTRAN proved that you don't sacrifice power when you raise the level of abstraction. One line could generate dozens of machine instructions — almost as fast as hand-written code. This shattered the myth that high-level languages were toys. FORTRAN is still in use today, over 65 years later, in scientific computing and weather modeling.
FORTRAN spoke the language of science. But the business world — banks, insurance companies, the government — needed a language that spoke English. And Grace Hopper had a vision for exactly that.
